question: NPC: Before we begin — inheritance in brief
intro: I'm Zoya, the Golem-Shaper. Every golem in this foundry begins from an older mould, and a Java class can begin from an older class too. Learn the words for that.

steps.say: **Inheritance** lets one class start from another and add to it. The older class is the **superclass**, or parent. The new one is the **subclass**. The keyword **extends** joins them: Kayak extends Boat. A subclass should pass the **is-a** test, and a kayak is a boat.

beats.say: **Inheritance** lets one class start from another and add to it. The older class is the **superclass**, or parent. The new one is the **subclass**.
The keyword **extends** joins them: Kayak extends Boat. A subclass should pass the **is-a** test, and a kayak is a boat.

check.prompt: In  class Raft extends Boat { },  which class is the superclass?
check.why: The class after extends is the one inherited from, so Boat is the superclass and Raft is the subclass.

steps.say: A subclass **inherits** its superclass's accessible fields and methods: it starts with them, then adds its own. A private member belongs to its own class alone, so a subclass cannot touch it directly. Constructors are not inherited either.

beats.say: A subclass **inherits** its superclass's accessible fields and methods: it starts with them, then adds its own.

figure.alt: A class diagram. Boat, with the method name() : String, is at the top. Below it are Kayak, with its own method paddle() : void highlighted, and Raft, with no members of its own. A hollow-triangle arrow points from each of them up to Boat.
figure.caption: Each arrow points up to the superclass.

beats.say: A private member belongs to its own class alone, so a subclass cannot touch it directly. Constructors are not inherited either.

steps.say: To **override** a method, the subclass writes one with the same name and the same parameters, but a new body. **@Override** asks the compiler to check that the method really replaces an inherited one.

beats.say: To **override** a method, the subclass writes one with the same name and the same parameters, but a new body.
**@Override** asks the compiler to check that the method really replaces an inherited one.

check.prompt: With the Kayak above, what does  new Kayak().name()  return?
check.why: The Kayak version overrides the inherited one, and a Kayak object always uses its own.

steps.say: Inside a subclass, **super** means the superclass part of the object. super.name()  runs Boat's version, so  new Kayak().name()  now returns "fast boat". In a constructor,  super(...)  runs the superclass's constructor.

beats.say: Inside a subclass, **super** means the superclass part of the object.
super.name()  runs Boat's version, so  new Kayak().name()  now returns "fast boat".
In a constructor,  super(...)  runs the superclass's constructor.

outro: Superclass, subclass, override, super. Now show the foundry what you know.

question:
Which keyword completes this header so that Dog becomes a subclass of Animal?
class Dog ___ Animal { }
incorrect: implements
inherits
super
feedback: class Dog extends Animal { } makes Dog a subclass of Animal: Dog gets Animal's accessible fields and methods (though not its constructors). implements is the keyword for interfaces, inherits is what some other languages use but is not Java, and super is used inside a subclass to reach the parent's constructor or methods.

question: Trace the inherited method. What does this print?
feedback: Dog never declares name(), but it extends Animal, so every Dog has Animal's name() as well as its own trick(). Inheritance means the subclass starts with what the parent has and then adds to it.

question: Inheritance should model an "is-a" relationship. Which of these headers is a sound use of extends?
incorrect: class Car extends Engine
class Knight extends Sword
class Library extends Book
feedback: A sword is a weapon, so Sword extends Weapon makes sense: anywhere a Weapon is expected, a Sword will do. A car HAS an engine, a knight HAS a sword and a library HAS books - those are "has-a" relationships, which you model with a field (Car holds an Engine field), not with extends.

question: After the keyword extends, how many parent classes may a Java class header name at most? (Type a number.) ___
feedback: Java has single inheritance of classes: class Dog extends Animal, Robot { } does not compile. Every class has exactly one direct parent class. (Interfaces are different - a class may implement several - and that is how Java gets most of the benefit without the ambiguity of two parents supplying the same method.)

correct: new Dog().eat() compiles, because Dog inherits the eat() method
A Dog object still contains an hp field, though Dog's code cannot name it
incorrect: new Dog("Rex") compiles, because Dog inherits Animal(String name)
Code inside Dog can read the private field by writing super.hp
Dog could gain a second parent class with extends Animal, Robot
feedback: Methods are inherited, so eat() works on a Dog. Constructors are NOT inherited: an empty Dog gets only a no-argument constructor, so new Dog("Rex") is a compile error. Private fields are still part of every Dog object (Animal's own methods use them) but are not accessible from Dog's code, with or without super. And a class may extend just one class.

figure.alt: A class diagram. Animal lists the field - hp : int, then + Animal(), + Animal(name : String) and + eat() : void. Below it, Dog has no members of its own, with a hollow-triangle arrow up to Animal.

question: name is a private field of PixarCharacter, which also has a public getName(). Inside a method of  class Toy extends PixarCharacter,  which line compiles?
incorrect: return name + " plays";
return this.name + " plays";
return super.name + " plays";
feedback: A Toy object does contain a name, but private means private to the class that declares it, and Toy is a different class. However the field is written, Toy may not touch it. The public getter is inherited, so getName() is the way in. (Had the field been protected, the first two would compile.)

question: What does a call such as super(name) inside a subclass constructor do?
correct: Runs the parent class's constructor, so the inherited fields get set up
incorrect: Creates a separate parent object that the subclass object delegates to
Replaces the parent's constructor with the subclass's constructor
Returns a reference to the parent portion of the object being built
feedback: There is one object, with a parent part and a subclass part. super(...) runs the parent's constructor so the parent part is initialised by the class that owns it. If you write no super(...) call at all, Java inserts super() for you - which compiles only when the parent has a no-argument constructor. It returns nothing and it creates no second object.

question: Animal's only constructor is Animal(String name). Inside the constructor Dog(String name), write the statement that passes name up to Animal's constructor.
feedback: super(name); runs Animal(String name). Because Animal has no no-argument constructor, leaving this line out would not compile: the super() that Java inserts automatically would have nothing to call. Older Java insisted this call open the constructor; since Java 25 other statements may come before it, provided they do not use the object being built.

correct: Compile error: Java adds super(), and there is no such constructor
incorrect: It compiles, and the name of every Toy is simply left as null
It compiles, since Toy inherits the constructor that takes a name
Compile error: a subclass is not allowed fields of its own
feedback: A constructor that does not call super(…) gets super() added for it, with nothing in the parentheses. PixarCharacter has no constructor that takes nothing, so the class does not compile. Constructors are never inherited, and Java will not guess what to pass. The fix is the missing first line: super(name);

question: NPC: Who gets built first?
intro: A Dog is an Animal with extras. So when I ask for a new Dog, which constructor do you think finishes first?

steps.say: Here are two classes. Each constructor prints one letter, so we can watch the order. Notice that Dog's constructor never mentions super.

beats.say: Here are two classes. Each constructor prints one letter, so we can watch the order.
Notice that Dog's constructor never mentions super.

steps.say: When a constructor has no **super(...)** call, the compiler quietly adds  super();  as its first line. So the Dog constructor that really runs is this one: super();  runs Animal's constructor, all of it, before the line below.

beats.say: When a constructor has no **super(...)** call, the compiler quietly adds  super();  as its first line. So the Dog constructor that really runs is this one:
super();  runs Animal's constructor, all of it, before the line below.

check.prompt: So what does new Dog(); print?
check.why: The hidden super() runs Animal's constructor first, printing A. Then the rest of Dog's constructor prints D.

steps.say: This is **constructor chaining**: each constructor first hands control to its parent's, up to Object at the top. Then the bodies run on the way back down. So the parent part of the object is ready before the subclass part builds on it: foundations first, then the extras.

beats.say: This is **constructor chaining**: each constructor first hands control to its parent's, up to Object at the top. Then the bodies run on the way back down.

figure.alt: Two columns. On the left, new Dog() leads up to Dog(), and arrows labelled super() climb to Animal() and then to Object(), which prints nothing. From there the right column runs down: Animal's body prints A, Dog's body prints D, and then the chain is done.
figure.caption: Up the chain first, then back down.

beats.say: So the parent part of the object is ready before the subclass part builds on it: foundations first, then the extras.

outro: The next monster has three generations in its family, not two. Same rule: follow the chain to the top, then come back down.

question: Trace the constructors. What does this print?
feedback: None of these constructors writes super(...), so the compiler adds super() to each. Sword's constructor starts by running Weapon's, which starts by running Item's (which in turn runs Object's). Item prints I, control returns to Weapon which prints W, and finally Sword prints S: the chain always completes from the top of the family tree downwards.

question: You write a chain of {{d}} classes: each one extends the class before it, and each has a single no-argument constructor that prints exactly one line. A loop then creates {{n}} objects of the LAST class in the chain. How many lines are printed in total?
feedback_template: Creating one object of the last class runs every constructor in the chain once, from the top class down: {{d}} lines per object. With {{n}} objects that is {{expected}} lines. Building a subclass object runs its parents' constructors as well as its own.

question: The subclass hands a value up to the superclass. What does this print?
feedback: super(name) runs Figure's constructor, which stores "Rex" in the name field that every Figure has. Then Toy's constructor stores its own extra field. getName() was written once, in Figure, and a Toy inherits it; tag() is Toy's own, and has to call getName() because name is private to Figure.

question: A private member is hidden even from subclasses. The access modifier that opens a member to subclasses (and to classes in the same package) while still hiding it from unrelated classes in other packages is ___.
feedback: protected sits between package-private (no modifier) and public: the same package can see it, and so can subclasses wherever they live. It is the usual choice for a field or helper method that a parent class wants its subclasses - but not the whole world - to use. Many designs still keep fields private and give subclasses a protected getter instead.

question: What does it mean for a subclass to override a method?
correct: It gives an inherited method a new body, keeping the same name and parameters
incorrect: It adds extra parameters to a method that it inherits from its parent class
It defines two methods with the same name but different parameter lists
It declares a field with the same name, which hides the parent's method
feedback: An override has the same name and the same parameter types as the inherited method, and supplies a different body; objects of the subclass then use the new version. Changing the parameters does not override anything - it creates a separate method alongside the inherited one. Fields and methods live in separate namespaces, so a field cannot replace a method.

correct: Compile error: speek() does not override anything
incorrect: It prints ... because speek() is a separate new method
It prints woof because @Override links speek() to speak()
It compiles, then throws an exception when speak() runs
feedback: @Override asks the compiler to confirm that the method really replaces an inherited one. Animal has no speek(), so compilation stops with "method does not override or implement a method from a supertype". Delete the annotation and the typo goes unnoticed: the program compiles and prints ... because Dog merely gained an unrelated method. That silent failure is why you write @Override on every override.

Overloading: one class, same name, DIFFERENT parameter lists - the compiler picks between play(int) and play(String) from the argument's type, at compile time. Overriding: a subclass, same name, SAME parameter list - the choice between Bard's and Skald's play(int) is made at run time from the object's actual class.

incorrect: @Override private Animal mate() { ... }
@Override protected Animal mate(int n) { ... }
@Override protected Object mate() { ... }
feedback: An override keeps the name and parameter list. It may make the method MORE visible (protected to public) and may return a more specific type (Dog is an Animal, so callers expecting an Animal are still satisfied). It may not make the method less visible (private), may not return a broader type (Object), and mate(int n) has a different parameter list, so it is an overload - which @Override then rejects.

question: Trace the calls that go through super. What does this print?
feedback: super.tag() calls the parent's version of an overridden method, so an override can build on the inherited behaviour rather than throw it away. C's tag() is "C" + B's tag(); B's tag() is A's tag() + "B", which is "AB". Put together: "C" + "AB" = CAB. Where each class puts its own letter - before or after the super call - decides the order.

question: class Gem { } declares nothing at all, yet System.out.println(new Gem()) prints text such as Gem@1b6d3586. Where does the toString() method that produced this text come from?
correct: Gem inherits it from Object, the root of every class
incorrect: The compiler writes one into every class as it compiles it
println builds the text itself when a class has no toString()
Gem inherits it from String, since println works with Strings
feedback: A class with no extends clause silently extends java.lang.Object, so every object has Object's methods - toString(), equals() and hashCode() among them. Object's toString() returns the class name, @, and a hash code in hexadecimal. When you write your own toString() you are overriding that inherited method, which is why it takes @Override and has to be public.

question: Hero wants its own equals, so that a.equals(b) and list.contains(…) compare names. Which first line OVERRIDES the equals that every object already has?
incorrect: public boolean equals(Hero other)
boolean equals(Object obj)
public boolean isEqual(Object obj)
feedback: To override a method you match its parameter list, and the equals inherited from Object takes an Object. equals(Hero other) is a different method with the same name, an overload: contains() would go on calling the inherited one. Without public the method is harder to reach than the one it replaces, which Java rejects. And another name replaces nothing. @Override catches all three slips.

question: This class overrides equals to compare names. What does the program print?
feedback: a and b are two separate objects, so == (the very same object?) is false, and nothing a class writes can change that. equals is a method, and this class has replaced the inherited one: it checks that the other object is a Hero, casts it so that its name can be read, and compares the two names. Same name, so true.

question: NPC: The label and the golem
intro: I have hung a wooden tag reading Golem around the neck of this hulking stone figure. The tag and the one wearing it are allowed to disagree, a little.

steps.say: Two classes. StoneGolem overrides greet() and adds a method of its own, smash(). The tag is g's **declared type**, Golem. The golem wearing it is the object, whose **runtime type** is StoneGolem. That is legal because a StoneGolem is a Golem.

beats.say: Two classes. StoneGolem overrides greet() and adds a method of its own, smash().
The tag is g's **declared type**, Golem. The golem wearing it is the object, whose **runtime type** is StoneGolem. That is legal because a StoneGolem is a Golem.

figure.alt: On the left, the variable g with its declared type, Golem. An arrow leads from it to an object on the right whose runtime type is StoneGolem.
figure.caption: The tag says Golem; the object is a StoneGolem.

steps.say: Rule one, at **run time**: the object decides which version of an overridden method runs. Java starts looking in the object's own class, StoneGolem, and finds its override there. That is **dynamic dispatch**. Using one variable type for many kinds of object is **polymorphism**.

beats.say: Rule one, at **run time**: the object decides which version of an overridden method runs.

beats.code:
Golem g = new StoneGolem();
System.out.println(g.greet());   // GRIND

beats.say: Java starts looking in the object's own class, StoneGolem, and finds its override there. That is **dynamic dispatch**.
Using one variable type for many kinds of object is **polymorphism**.

steps.say: Rule two, at **compile time**: the compiler sees only the tag. It checks each call against the declared type, Golem, and nothing else.

beats.say: Rule two, at **compile time**: the compiler sees only the tag. It checks each call against the declared type, Golem, and nothing else.

check.answer: Compile error: Golem has no smash()
wrong: It compiles, then fails at run time
check.why: The compiler looks at the declared type, Golem, which has no smash(). It does not matter that the object happens to be a StoneGolem.

steps.say: So the declared type decides what you may call, and the runtime type decides which version runs.

beats.say: So the declared type decides what you may call, and the runtime type decides which version runs.

figure.alt: Two class boxes side by side. On the left, under the heading compile time: look in the declared type, is Golem, with greet() : String highlighted and nothing else. On the right, under run time: look in the object's class, is StoneGolem, with its own greet() : String highlighted, and smash() : void.
figure.caption: Two questions, two classes to look in.

outro: Animals next, not golems. Ask both questions of every line: what does the tag allow, and who is really wearing it?

question: Trace the two calls through Animal variables. What does this print?
feedback: Both variables are declared as Animal, but the objects differ. a refers to a Dog, and Dog overrides sound(), so the runtime type picks woof. b refers to a Cat, which does not override sound(), so it uses the version it inherited from Animal. The declared type did not choose either result.

correct: Compile error: the type Animal has no fetch() method
incorrect: It prints got it, since the object really is a Dog
It compiles, then throws a ClassCastException at run time
It compiles, then throws a NoSuchMethodError at run time
feedback: The compiler checks a call against the variable's declared type. a is an Animal, and Animal has no fetch(), so the line is rejected ("cannot find symbol") before anything runs - the compiler does not reason about which object a will hold. To call fetch() you need a reference whose type is Dog.

correct: woof: a cast changes how the reference is typed, not what the object is
incorrect: ...: the cast to Animal makes the call use Animal's version of speak()
...: the compiler picks speak() from the type that is written in the cast
Compile error: a Dog reference may not be cast upward to its parent type
feedback: A cast never changes the object; it only changes the type the compiler uses for that expression. The object is still a Dog, and an overridden method is chosen from the object's runtime class, so Dog's speak() runs. Casting up to a parent type is legal (and unnecessary - it happens automatically). The way to reach a parent's version is super.speak(), and only from inside the subclass.

pairs.definition: Compiles with no cast, since moving up the family tree is safe
Needs its cast to compile, then succeeds when run
Compiles, then throws ClassCastException when run

feedback: Going up (Dog to Animal to Object) is automatic. Going down needs an explicit cast, because the compiler knows only that a is some Animal; without the cast, Dog d = a; is rejected. With a cast the compiler trusts you and the check moves to run time: a really holds a Dog, so it succeeds, while c holds a Cat, so the JVM throws ClassCastException.

figure.alt: A class diagram of a family tree. Object is at the top. Animal is below it, with a hollow-triangle arrow up to Object. Dog and Cat are side by side below Animal, each with a hollow-triangle arrow up to Animal.

feedback_template: The loop only ever sees the declared type Shape, but each call to sides() runs the version belonging to the actual object: 3 for every Triangle and 4 for every Square. {{t}} triangles give 3 x {{t}} and {{s}} squares give 4 x {{s}}, so total is {{expected}}. One loop, no if statements - that is what polymorphism buys you.

question: NPC: Ask before you cast
intro: See that golem shuffling past, wearing the plain Golem tag? Suppose I am sure that one is stone. Watch what my certainty is worth.

steps.say: The **cast**  (StoneGolem)  is my promise to the compiler that g holds a StoneGolem. So it compiles. But at run time the object is clay, the promise is false, and the program dies with a **ClassCastException**.

figure.alt: A class diagram. Golem is at the top. Below it are StoneGolem, which has the method smash() : void, and ClayGolem, which has no members. A hollow-triangle arrow points from each up to Golem.
figure.caption: Only StoneGolem has smash().

beats.say: The **cast**  (StoneGolem)  is my promise to the compiler that g holds a StoneGolem. So it compiles.
But at run time the object is clay, the promise is false, and the program dies with a **ClassCastException**.

steps.say: So ask first. The **instanceof** operator tests an object's runtime type, and modern Java lets you name a new variable right inside the test. If g holds a StoneGolem, then s is that same object, already typed as StoneGolem, with no cast to write. This form is called a **type pattern**.

beats.say: So ask first. The **instanceof** operator tests an object's runtime type, and modern Java lets you name a new variable right inside the test.
If g holds a StoneGolem, then s is that same object, already typed as StoneGolem, with no cast to write. This form is called a **type pattern**.

check.prompt: g still holds a ClayGolem. What does this if statement do?
check.answer: Skips the block; nothing is thrown
wrong: Runs smash() on the clay golem
check.why: instanceof simply answers false when the object is not a StoneGolem, so the block is skipped. Asking is safe; only a wrong cast throws.

steps.say: Older code does the same in two steps: test with instanceof, then cast on the next line. You will still read that. The pattern form says it once, and cannot get the cast wrong.

beats.say: Older code does the same in two steps: test with instanceof, then cast on the next line.

figure.alt: A flowchart. A diamond asks: g instanceof StoneGolem? Its true branch leads to cast safely, then s.smash(), highlighted. Its false branch leads to skip the block, dimmed.
figure.caption: Ask first; cast only on true.

beats.say: You will still read that. The pattern form says it once, and cannot get the cast wrong.

outro: Your turn to write one. A different creature, the same safe question first.

question: The variable a is declared as Animal. Write the condition - just the expression that goes inside the parentheses of an if - that is true when a holds a Dog and, in that case, binds the Dog to a new variable named d.
feedback: a instanceof Dog d tests the runtime type and, when the test passes, declares d as a Dog referring to the same object - so inside the if you can write d.fetch() with no cast. The older two-step form, if (a instanceof Dog) { Dog d = (Dog) a; ... }, still works and you will meet it in older code.

question: instanceof asks what an object really is. What does this print?
feedback: Every element is held in a Figure variable, but instanceof looks at the object. Three of the five are Toys. The Monster and the plain Figure are not, so they are counted as others. The last line asks whether a Monster is a Figure: it is, because Monster extends Figure, and instanceof is true for the object's own class and for everything above it.

question: A method only Toy has is reached by checking, then casting. What does this print?
feedback: f.perform() runs Toy's version, because the object is a Toy: pose. But f.play() would not compile, since the variable's type is Figure and Figure has no play(). So the code first asks whether the object is a Toy, then casts: t is the same object, held in a Toy variable, and play() can be called through it.

incorrect: a instanceof Cat
n instanceof Animal
feedback: instanceof asks about the object, not the variable: the object is a Dog, and a Dog is also an Animal, a Pet (through implements) and an Object, so all four are true. It is not a Cat - sharing a parent does not make siblings interchangeable. And n refers to no object at all, so instanceof answers false for null whatever n's declared type says; that is why no separate null check is needed before it.

question: What does the keyword abstract mean when it is applied to a class?
correct: The class cannot be instantiated with new; it exists to be extended
incorrect: Each of its methods has to be abstract, declared without a body
The class may hold method signatures but no constructors or fields
The class is closed to extension and has to be used as written
feedback: An abstract class is an unfinished parent: new Shape() is a compile error, and objects come from its concrete subclasses. It MAY contain abstract methods, but it can also have ordinary methods, fields and constructors - the description with signatures and nothing else fits an interface. A class closed to extension is a final class, the opposite idea.

question: public abstract int wheels(); is a complete declaration of an abstract method. Compared with an ordinary method, the thing it lacks is a ___.
feedback: An abstract method ends in a semicolon where an ordinary method has { ... }. It states the name, parameters and return type, and leaves the body to each concrete subclass - which the compiler then insists on.

question: Which statements about an abstract class Shape are correct?
correct: Shape may mix abstract methods with ordinary methods that have bodies
Shape may declare a constructor, which subclasses run through super(...)
A variable of type Shape may refer to an object of a concrete subclass
incorrect: new Shape() compiles, but throws an exception once the program runs
A concrete subclass may skip an abstract method that it does not call
feedback: An abstract class can hold fields, constructors and finished methods next to its abstract ones, and Shape s = new Circle(); is the normal way to use it. new Shape() is rejected by the compiler ("Shape is abstract; cannot be instantiated"), not at run time. A subclass that leaves any abstract method without a body does not compile unless it is declared abstract itself - whether the method is called is irrelevant.

question: Trace the abstract class. What does this print?
feedback: describe() is written once, in the abstract parent, and calls wheels() - a method Vehicle itself leaves unfinished. When describe() runs on a Trike, that inner call is dispatched to the object's runtime class, so Trike's wheels() supplies 3. This is the main use of an abstract class: shared code in the parent, with the varying step filled in by each subclass.

question:
interface Drawable { void draw(); }
An interface lists methods that a class promises to supply. Circle makes that promise with the header: class Circle ___ Drawable
feedback: A class implements an interface and extends a class; mixing the two up is a compile error. Having made the promise, Circle has to provide a public draw() method, and a Circle can then be used wherever a Drawable is expected: Drawable d = new Circle();

question:
PixarCharacter is a class. Quotable and Rescuable are interfaces. Complete the header.
public class Superhero {{1}} PixarCharacter {{2}} Quotable{{3}} Rescuable {
feedback: A class extends one class and implements any number of interfaces, in that order, with the interfaces separated by commas. Superhero then inherits what PixarCharacter has, and owes a public method for everything Quotable and Rescuable list.

question: Trace the interface and its default method. What does this print?
feedback: name() has no body, so every implementing class has to supply it. greet() is a default method: the interface gives it a body, which implementing classes inherit unless they override it. Elf inherits it, so its greeting is "hi " plus Elf's own name(). Orc overrides it and prints grr - its name() is never used.

question: Which statements about Java interfaces are correct?
correct: A class may implement several interfaces in the same header
A default method's body is inherited by the implementing classes
incorrect: A class may leave some of an interface's abstract methods out and still be instantiated
An interface may declare a constructor for its implementing classes to call
An interface may declare instance fields, so each implementing object gets a copy
new Drawable() creates an object, provided every method has a default body
feedback: class Duck implements Swimmer, Flyer { } is legal, and default methods come along for free. An interface has no constructors and no per-object fields (any field in an interface is a static final constant), and it can never be instantiated with new, however many default methods it has. A class that skips an abstract method of its interface does not compile unless it is declared abstract.

question: Two classes with nothing else in common implement one interface. What does this print?
feedback: An interface is a type, so a Performer[] can hold any object whose class implements Performer, whatever else those classes are. The loop calls perform() on each, and each object runs its own class's version. Toy and Robot share no superclass here; the interface is all they have in common, and all the loop needs.

question: An abstract class and an interface both leave methods for other classes to finish, but they differ. Of the two, the one that can declare constructors and instance fields is the {{1}}. The one that a class can combine with several others of its kind in a single header is the {{2}}. And when a class supplies a method promised by an interface, it has to give that method the access modifier {{3}}.
feedback: An abstract class is still a class: it has state and constructors, and a subclass may extend just one class. An interface carries no per-object state, which is what makes it safe to implement many at once. Interface methods are public automatically, and an implementing method may not be less visible than the one it implements - leave off public and the compiler reports "attempting to assign weaker access privileges".

question: Bird extends Animal, and Plane extends Vehicle. Both need a fly() method, and one loop should be able to call fly() on a list that mixes birds and planes. Which design works?
correct: Declare an interface Flyer and have both classes implement it
incorrect: Declare an abstract class Flyer and have both classes extend it too
Make Plane extend Bird, so that Plane inherits Bird's fly() method
Put them in a List<Object> and call fly() on each element in turn
feedback: Bird and Plane already have parent classes, and a class can extend just one, so a second parent class Flyer is impossible. A plane is not a bird, so Plane extends Bird abuses is-a (and Plane already has a parent). A List<Object> compiles only until you call fly(): the declared type Object has no such method. An interface is the tool for a shared ability across unrelated classes: List<Flyer> holds both, and fly() is callable on every element.

question: Arrange these lines from top to bottom so that every name is declared before the line that uses it, ending with the line that prints 3.
items: class Tri implements Shape { public int sides() { return 3; } }
feedback: The interface comes first because Tri's header names it. Tri has to exist before new Tri() can build one, and s has to hold an object before s.sides() can be called. Note that the variable's type is the interface, and that Tri's sides() is public because interface methods are public.

question: NPC: Building on a class you did not write
intro: This finished class is the superclass, and it is not yours to change. Your subclass gets everything it has, and whatever you add.

steps.say: Its only **constructor** takes a name, so your subclass's constructor has to hand one up. Begin it with  super(name);  and this one runs first.

beats.say: Its only **constructor** takes a name, so your subclass's constructor has to hand one up. Begin it with  super(name);  and this one runs first.

check.why: The field is private to PixarCharacter, so neither this.name nor super.name compiles in Toy. The public getter is inherited, and can be called with nothing in front of it.

steps.say: When you **override** a method, or write one that an interface or an abstract class asks for, copy its first line exactly: the same name, the same parameters, the same return type. Every class inherits  public String toString()  from Object. So Toy's override starts with that same line: If the one above is public, yours has to be public too. Leave public off and the compiler stops you: a method that replaces another cannot be harder to reach.

question: Write the body of Toy's constructor. The name and the movie belong to the PixarCharacter part of the object, so hand them up; the owner is Toy's own.
signature: Toy(String name, String movie, String owner)

tests.expect: Hi! I'm Woody from Toy Story.

tests.run:
Toy a = new Toy("Rex", "Toy Story", "Andy");
Toy b = new Toy("Forky", "Toy Story 4", "Bonnie");

hint: First line: super(name, movie); That runs PixarCharacter's constructor. Then store the owner with this.owner.
feedback: PixarCharacter keeps name and movie private, and has a constructor that sets them, so the subclass passes them up with super(…). Only then does Toy deal with the one field it added. Leave super(…) out and Java tries super() with nothing in it, which PixarCharacter does not have.

question: Override introduce() so that a Toy says everything a PixarCharacter says and then who it belongs to:  Hi! I'm Woody from Toy Story. I belong to Andy!  Use the superclass's version for the first part.

tests.expect: Hi! I'm Woody from Toy Story. I belong to Andy!
Hi! I'm Rex from Toy Story. I belong to Bonnie!
Hi! I'm Joy from Inside Out.

solution: return super.introduce() + " I belong to " + owner + "!";
hint: super.introduce() gives back the sentence PixarCharacter makes. Add the rest to it with +.
feedback: super.introduce() runs the version this method replaces, so the Toy builds on the superclass's sentence instead of copying it. The second test holds the Toy in a PixarCharacter variable and still gets the Toy's sentence: the object decides which version runs.

A constructor  Fish(String name, String movie, String habitat)  that hands the first two up.
String swim()  returns  Nemo swims through the coral reef!

tests.run: Fish nemo = new Fish("Nemo", "Finding Nemo", "coral reef");
tests.expect: Nemo swims through the coral reef!

tests.run: Fish bruce = new Fish("Bruce", "Finding Nemo", "open ocean");

Fish b = new Fish("B", "m", "pond");
tests.expect: A swims through the sea!B swims through the pond!

hint: Only habitat is Fish's to declare. The name is reached with getName(), which Fish inherits.
feedback: A subclass declares only what it adds. The name and the movie live in the PixarCharacter part, set by super(name, movie) and read back with the inherited getter; introduce() comes along with no code at all.

question: Override equals. Two Superheroes are equal when they have the same name AND the same power; strength does not count. Anything that is not a Superhero, null included, is not equal.

tests.run:
Superhero a = new Superhero("Dash", "Speed", 70);
Superhero b = new Superhero("Dash", "Speed", 5);

Superhero a = new Superhero("Dash", "Speed", 70);
Superhero b = new Superhero("Dash", "Ice", 70);

Superhero a = new Superhero("Dash", "Speed", 70);
Superhero b = new Superhero("Violet", "Speed", 70);

ArrayList<Superhero> team = new ArrayList<>();
team.add(new Superhero("Dash", "Speed", 70));

hint: Rule out what is not a Superhero with instanceof (null is not one). Then cast, and compare the two Strings with .equals().
feedback: The parameter is an Object, so it could be anything; instanceof rules out other classes, and null with them. After the cast the other hero's private fields can be read, because both objects are of this class. The last test shows the point of overriding: contains() calls equals, and now finds a hero who merely looks the same.

question: Write findStrongest. It returns the Superhero in the array with the highest strength level. If the array is empty, it returns null.

tests.run: Superhero[] hs = { new Superhero("A", "a", 5), new Superhero("B", "b", 50), new Superhero("C", "c", 9) };
Superhero[] hs = { new Superhero("A", "a", 95), new Superhero("B", "b", 50) };

hint: Keep the best hero so far in a variable that starts as null. A hero beats it if there is no best yet, or its strength is higher.
feedback: The find-the-largest pattern, keeping the whole object rather than just the number. It is static because it is not about one hero: it is called on the class, Superhero.findStrongest(…). Starting best at null handles the empty array, and a hero whose strength is negative.

perform()  returns  Sulley scares with power 9!
hint: perform() is abstract above, so Monster has to write it, and as public, with exactly the same first line.

question: Write runParade. For each character in the array, in order, add two lines to the result: its toString(), then its perform(). After them add one last line of the form  Parade: 2 toys, 1 monsters.  Put "\n" between lines, with none after the last.

tests.run: PixarCharacter[] cast = { new Toy("Woody", "Toy Story"), new Monster("Sulley", "Monsters, Inc.") };
tests.expect:
Woody (Toy Story)
Woody comes to life!
Sulley (Monsters, Inc.)
Sulley roars!
Parade: 1 toys, 1 monsters

tests.run: PixarCharacter[] cast = { new Toy("A", "x"), new Toy("B", "x"), new Monster("C", "y") };
tests.expect:
A (x)
A comes to life!
B (x)
B comes to life!
C (y)
C roars!

M (z)

hint: One loop. perform() needs no if: each object runs its own. Only the counting needs instanceof.
feedback: The loop calls perform() without knowing or caring which kind of character it has; that is polymorphism. instanceof is kept for the one job that really is about the kind: the count. Putting "\n" after every character line, and none after the summary, gives exactly one line break between lines.

question:
Write the class Rock. GameObject and Drawable are given above.
One private field:  int x.
A constructor  Rock(String name, int x).
draw()  returns  [Rock Boulder at 4]
update()  rolls the rock one step to the right: it adds 1 to x.
signature: class Rock extends GameObject implements Drawable
hint: Two methods are owed: draw() to Drawable, and update() to GameObject. Both have to be public.
feedback: One class, two promises. It extends GameObject, which requires update(); it implements Drawable, which requires draw(). The tests hold the same object as a Drawable and as a GameObject: each type allows only its own methods, and each call runs Rock's code.
